name: Cistanche
lead: Cistanche is a genus of parasitic desert plants whose fleshy stems, chiefly from Cistanche deserticola and Cistanche tubulosa, are used as a tonic in traditional Chinese medicine under the name Rou Cong Rong, sometimes called "desert ginseng" [1][5][4]. Traditional uses include treating kidney deficiency, impotence, female infertility and constipation in older people [4].

In bodybuilding and testosterone-optimisation communities, Cistanche tubulosa extract is sold as a herbal supplement and is described by some users as a test booster or a DHT booster, often stacked with other herbs during post-cycle therapy [19][20][21]. Laboratory and animal research has examined its phenylethanoid glycosides (echinacoside, acteoside) for antioxidant, neuroprotective, liver-protective and bone-related effects [1][7][6].

Human trials of Cistanche extracts are few and small. They have looked at muscle strength and recovery, locomotive function, cognition and fatigue [8][10][9][15]. No published trial identified here has measured testosterone-raising or DHT-raising effects as a cosmetic or physique outcome.
infobox: Wild C. deserticola is on CITES Appendix II; approved as a food ingredient in China from 2016 [2][3]

paras: The genus Cistanche belongs to the family Orobanchaceae. Its members lack chlorophyll and draw nutrients from the roots of host shrubs in arid regions [18]. The dried stems are the medicinal part [1].

Reviews describe the main active-compound classes as phenylethanoid glycosides, iridoids, lignans and polysaccharides [4][3]. Wild populations were once endangered, and large-scale cultivation has since turned the herb into a major commercial product in China, with an estimated annual output of about 6,000 tons [2].

In traditional Chinese medicine the herb is classed as a kidney-yang tonic. It is used for impotence, infertility, weakness of the lower back and knees, and constipation [4][5]. Modern review articles list proposed pharmacological actions such as anti-ageing, antioxidant, neuroprotective, hepatoprotective, immunomodulatory and bone-promoting effects, mostly from cell and animal work [1][5].

On the T Nation forum, users list Cistanche tubulosa among herbs added to post-cycle recovery or testosterone-support regimens alongside tongkat ali, ashwagandha, DIM and others [19][20]. One user lists it as a "DHT boost" in a supplement routine [21]. Another thread asks whether a list of herbs that includes Cistanche carries a risk of organ damage [22].

A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial published in 2025 enrolled 48 men, half resistance-trained and half untrained, to test Cistanche deserticola supplementation on muscle strength and recovery [8]. A related registration describes a study of Cistanche on anaerobic performance and recovery in men with different training levels [14].

Other randomized trials have tested Cistanche tubulosa extract on locomotive syndrome in older adults [9], a Cistanche tubulosa and Ginkgo biloba combination on cognitive function in middle-aged and older people [10][11], and a Ginkgo and Cistanche product on fatigue symptoms [15]. A trial in men with central obesity combined an extract with aerobic exercise [16]. A Chinese granule formula was tested for tinnitus in chronic nephritis [12].

A 2025 systematic review and network meta-analysis of dietary supplements for androgenetic alopecia is listed among related literature, but the summary available does not report Cistanche-specific findings [13]. No trial found here has tested Cistanche for testosterone or DHT levels as a primary outcome.

Traditional use and Chinese food-ingredient approval are cited in reviews as indications of acceptable tolerability [3], but the human trials above are small and short. A forum thread raises the question of organ damage from herbal supplements including Cistanche, without presenting data [22]. A topical herbal patch containing Cistanche deserticola is listed in the US DailyMed database as an unapproved product marketed for prostate-related symptoms [17].

timeline.event: Antioxidant phenylethanoids isolated from Cistanche deserticola are characterised [6].
China's food-safety agency approves Cistanche for use as a food ingredient [3].
Randomized trial of Cistanche tubulosa extract in locomotive syndrome is published [9].
Randomized trial of Cistanche deserticola on strength and recovery is published [8].

lore.intro: Cistanche appears mainly in testosterone-support and post-cycle herb lists on bodybuilding forums rather than in appearance-focused discussion [19][20][21].

claims.claim: Cistanche tubulosa extract is a "DHT boost" or test booster
claims.believers: Some forum users include it in routines intended to raise androgens or support recovery after a cycle and report taking it alongside other herbs [20][21].
claims.experts: Reviews describe antioxidant, neuroprotective and tonic activities studied mostly in cells and animals; no human trial found here measured testosterone or DHT as a main outcome [1][3].

claims.claim: Cistanche helps libido and erectile function after a cycle
claims.believers: One user lists it among herbs tried to restore libido after prolonged use of a nandrolone-type steroid [19].
claims.experts: Traditional medicine uses it for impotence [4]; the human trials located here address strength, cognition, fatigue and other outcomes, not sexual function [8][10][9].

claims.claim: Cistanche improves muscle strength and recovery
claims.believers: Supplement users group it with performance and recovery herbs [21].
claims.experts: A randomized placebo-controlled trial in 48 men studied this question, and a second trial is registered; the available summaries do not detail the effect sizes [8][14].

claims.claim: Herbal blends including Cistanche may harm organs
claims.believers: A forum poster asks whether herbs on a list, Cistanche among them, can cause organ damage [22].
claims.experts: No cited trial reported organ toxicity from Cistanche; reviews note its food-ingredient approval in China [3].

card.summary: A Chinese tonic herb that bodybuilding forums list as a test and DHT booster; human trials on those claims are essentially absent.
card.aka: Rou Cong Rong, desert ginseng, Cistanche tubulosa extract
card.note: Small human trials exist for strength, cognition and fatigue; none found for testosterone or DHT.

quick.overview:
Cistanche is the dried stem of a parasitic desert plant used for centuries in traditional Chinese medicine as a kidney and vitality tonic. Extracts are sold as supplements.

In forums it is mentioned as a testosterone or DHT booster and as part of post-cycle herb stacks. The research available is mostly lab and animal work, plus a few small trials on strength, cognition and fatigue.
quick.mechanism: Its phenylethanoid glycosides such as echinacoside and acteoside show antioxidant and neuroprotective effects in cell and animal studies. How, or whether, this would change androgen levels in people has not been shown in trials found here.
quick.risks: Trials reported so far are small and short, and it is approved as a food ingredient in China. Long-term safety data in healthy men are limited, and wild C. deserticola is on CITES Appendix II.
